prompt: In some areas, libraries, parks and community centres that were once run by paid council staff are now managed by local volunteers. Some people believe this is the best way to keep such services open, while others argue that local government should pay professionals to run them. Discuss both views and give your own opinion.
essay:
When a council can no longer afford to staff a library, the real choice is seldom between volunteers and professionals. It is between volunteers and a locked door, which is why the volunteer model has spread. The question worth asking is not whether residents can run these places — plainly they sometimes can — but which residents, and where.

Those who welcome the change have a strong case. A building kept open by its neighbours is better than one boarded up, and volunteers often bring a commitment that paid staff, moved between sites by a distant department, cannot match. They know which families use the reading room after school; they raise money, organise events and treat the place as their own, because in a real sense it now is. For those who have retired, the work can also supply both purpose and company.

Those who insist on paid staff are pointing to something less visible. A library is also where people without internet access apply for jobs, where someone defeated by an official form finds help, and where a trained eye notices that a regular visitor is no longer coping. That work depends on skill and on the same person being there next week, which a rota cannot promise. More fundamentally, the capacity to volunteer is not evenly spread. It belongs disproportionately to people with time, confidence and a secure income — to the retired professional rather than the parent working two jobs — so volunteer-run services tend to flourish in prosperous districts and quietly lapse in poor ones.

That last point settles the matter for me. Public services exist partly to ensure that what a neighbourhood receives does not depend on what it can supply for itself, and wholesale reliance on volunteers reverses that principle. Volunteers should certainly be welcomed, extending opening hours and running activities no budget would cover. But responsibility for whether a library or community centre exists at all should stay with the council, and where money is short it should be spent first in the places least able to replace it with goodwill.
title: Volunteers running local services
